title: What awe is
hookLine: the feeling of something vast that you can't quite take in; every tradition names it differently

cards: The edge of a canyon, where the ground simply stops. A thunderstorm rolling in over a lake. A newborn's whole hand wrapped around one finger.
A night sky so far from town that the stars look crowded. Some things don't fit. The mind tries to take them in and runs out of room.
For some, the breath catches; for others, there's stillness, or a laugh, or tears that make no sense. Then the moment passes.
For the weeks ahead, this path stays with that moment, starting with the plainest question: what is it?

teach.b: First, an old word with two sides. Some readers hear the old word fear, in lines like this one, as something closer to awe. The psalm says, in the King James words: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom".
Not terror that makes you run. More like standing very still because you've met something larger than you. Second, a scholar's name for it.
Rudolf Otto, a German writer on religion, described the holy as a mystery that makes people tremble and draws them in at the same time.
He used Latin for it: mysterium tremendum, a mystery that makes one tremble, and fascinans, what draws one in.
Third, the strange thing about awe: it's often about what was there all along.

Emerson, in his essay Nature, tries a thought experiment: "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore; and preserve for many generations the remembrance of the city of God which had been shown!"
And yet, he says, they come out every night, and we barely look. Fourth, the names. A psalm calls it glory.
Moses is told he stands on holy ground. Jacob wakes and says he didn't know. The Qur'an calls such things signs.
Each one gets its own day ahead, in its own words. Different words, one shared gesture underneath: looking up from what's in your hands to what's around you.

how: People on this path often mark awe by pausing outdoors, at the sea, on a mountain or under the night sky, and by reading the passages different traditions wrote about such moments.

o: a Latin name for a storm too big to measure
a holy mystery: you tremble, yet are drawn in
a fear of God that makes people run and hide

games.q: what awe is — tap the pairs.
p: stars once in a thousand years
from your hands to the world

s: in the psalm, the fear of the LORD means terror that makes you run
the same word can be heard as awe: standing still before something larger.
Otto described the holy as both terrible and fascinating
mysterium tremendum et fascinans: it makes people tremble and draws them in.
Emerson says awe needs a rare event
his point is that the stars come out every night, and we barely look.

games.q: Emerson asks: what if the stars appeared only one night in a thousand years? what does he say people would do?
o: believe and adore, and remember it for generations.
games.why: they would believe and adore, and keep the memory for generations. and yet, he says, the stars come out every night.

practice: Lift your eyes slowly above everything you usually look at, screens, faces, tables, to the sky if you have it, or a treetop, or just the ceiling and the light coming in.
For one minute, don't name what you see; let it be bigger than you, and let thoughts pass under it like birds. If you pray, the looking can be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Mysterium tremendum. Rudolf Otto's Latin for the holy: a mystery that makes one tremble and draws one in at once. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: fear, awe. the word behind "the fear of the LORD" in Psalm 111:10.

carryVoice: Your line: look up. The stars come out every night, whether anyone looks or not. One day short of a thousand.
